title: Nollywood
objective: After this level you can explain how Nigeria's film industry grew from cheap video films sold on cassettes in the 1990s.
summary: When the naira's fall ended celluloid filmmaking in Nigeria, Living in Bondage (1992) went straight to VHS and sparked a fast, low-budget video industry later called Nollywood.

cards.headline: A film industry built on videocassettes.
cards.body: In 1992, a Nigerian film called Living in Bondage skipped cinema screens. It went straight to VHS tape and became a smash hit. Why would a country's movies grow up on cassettes?

cards.headline: When celluloid slipped out of reach
cards.body: In the 1980s, Nigeria's currency, the naira, was devalued. Film equipment became hard to come by, and movie theaters grew harder and harder to reach. By the early 1990s, making films on celluloid had stopped altogether. If stories were going to reach people, they needed another road.

cards.headline: Straight to tape
cards.body: Living in Bondage took that road. Britannica dates Nigeria's video film industry to its 1992 release: sold straight to VHS, it became a hit and revolutionized Nigerian cinema. Others followed fast, on small budgets, most shot in about a week. The industry makes films in Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa and other Nigerian languages.

cards.headline: The name came later
cards.body: The industry was booming for a decade before it had its famous nickname. 'Nollywood', Nigeria plus Hollywood, first appeared in a New York Times headline in 2002. By then, the films had long been finding their audiences on tape.

mascot.line: Don't memorize every date. Remember the order: celluloid got out of reach, video stepped in, the name came last.

cards.headline: Nollywood: rolling
learned: The naira's fall ended celluloid filmmaking
Living in Bondage (1992) went straight to VHS
Fast, low-budget films in many languages

questions.prompt: How did Living in Bondage reach its audience in 1992?

options.label: Through a long run in new city cinemas
options.rationale: It skipped cinemas and went to tape.

options.label: At the Cannes film market
options.rationale: Its success came at home, on tape.

questions.explanation: Living in Bondage was distributed straight to VHS and became a smash hit.

questions.prompt: Why did Nigerian filmmaking turn from celluloid to video?

options.label: The naira's devaluation made equipment scarce and theaters hard to reach
The government banned film cameras and closed the film schools
options.rationale: The cause was economic, not a ban.

options.label: Audiences came to prefer black-and-white films shot on celluloid
options.rationale: The level describes costs and access, not taste.

options.label: Hollywood studios bought every cinema in Nigeria and shut them
options.rationale: Nothing in the level says so.

questions.explanation: After the naira was devalued in the 1980s, equipment became hard to get, theaters inaccessible, and celluloid production stopped.

questions.prompt: Level 5 explained that projection won because one film could serve a whole paying room. How did Nollywood's first hits reach people instead?

options.label: In peep-show cabinets, one viewer at a time
In grand projection halls built for them
options.rationale: Theaters had become hard to reach.

options.label: Through touring camera operators
options.rationale: That's how the Lumières spread cinema.

options.label: On videotapes people could take home

questions.explanation: With theaters out of reach, Nigerian films were sold straight to VHS for viewers to watch on their own screens.
